fable-5.1.text:
The main thing we learned is that a lot of what people were calling a "transformer advantage" wasn't really about attention at all. When we started the project, the narrative was that Swin Transformer beats ResNet, so attention must be better than convolution. But a ResNet-50 and a Swin-T differ in dozens of ways besides the operator, and nobody had carefully separated them.

So we did the boring thing. We took a plain ResNet-50 and changed one thing at a time, moving it toward the Swin design, and tracked accuracy at every step.

The first and biggest surprise was the training recipe alone. Just training the unchanged ResNet-50 with the modern procedure, meaning AdamW, a 300-epoch schedule, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth, label smoothing, closed roughly half of the gap. Nothing about the architecture changed. That told us a large part of the "ResNet is worse" story was really "ResNet was trained with a 2015 recipe."

Then the architectural changes each contributed a few tenths of a point. Changing the stage compute ratio to match Swin. Replacing the stem with a patchify layer. Switching to depthwise convolution, which is actually closer to what attention does, since it mixes spatially but per channel. Using the inverted bottleneck from the transformer MLP block. Moving the depthwise layer up and going to 7 by 7 kernels so each block sees a wider region. And then the micro details, fewer activations, fewer normalization layers, GELU instead of ReLU, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, separate downsampling layers.

None of these steps was dramatic on its own. But together they got a pure convnet to match and slightly exceed Swin at every scale, and it scaled fine with ImageNet-22K pretraining too.

So the honest conclusion is not that convolution is better than attention. It's that the comparison was confounded. The transformer papers brought a whole package of design and training improvements, and the community attributed the gain to the one component that was new and exciting. When you give the convnet the same package, the gap mostly disappears. Attention may still have real advantages in other settings, like multimodal models or very flexible input formats, but on standard vision benchmarks the inductive bias of convolution was never the problem.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says, “None of these steps was dramatic on its own,” directly stating that no individual ablation produced a large gain.

r002.rationale: The response explains that the combined training and architectural package eliminated the gap for a pure convnet, showing that these details mattered more than whether the core operation was convolution or attention.

opus-5.5.text:
Going in, the common belief was that self-attention itself was the reason vision transformers were pulling ahead. Once Swin Transformer came out and did well on detection and segmentation, people concluded that convolution had had its run. We weren't sure that was right. Every time a transformer beat a ConvNet, the comparison also changed many other things: the training recipe, the architecture's macro layout, the normalization, the activations. So the attribution was muddled.

What we did was simple. We took a standard ResNet-50 and modernized it one step at a time toward the design of a hierarchical vision transformer like Swin, without ever adding attention. We measured ImageNet accuracy and compute at every step, so we could see where the gains actually came from.

The first surprise was how much came from training alone. We used the transformer-style recipe: AdamW, 300 epochs instead of 90, and heavy augmentation and regularization like Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth and label smoothing. That took plain ResNet-50 from about 76 to almost 79 percent with no architecture change at all. A good part of the "transformer advantage" in earlier comparisons was really a training-recipe advantage.

Then the architecture changes each added a little:
- **Macro design.** We changed the stage compute ratio to match Swin and used a patchify stem, a 4×4 stride-4 conv, instead of the old aggressive stem with max pooling.
- **Depthwise convolution with wider channels.** This is close in spirit to how self-attention mixes spatial information per channel.
- **Inverted bottleneck.**
- **Larger kernels.** We moved up to 7×7 depthwise convolutions, which roughly matched Swin's window size, and gains saturated around there.
- **Micro design.** We used GELU, fewer activation and normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, and separate downsampling layers.

None of these choices were new on their own. They had all appeared somewhere. But together they took the pure ConvNet to about 82 percent at the tiny scale, slightly above Swin-T at similar compute. It also held up when we scaled model size and pretrained on ImageNet-22K, and on downstream detection and segmentation.

So my main takeaway is that the gap wasn't really about attention versus convolution. Much of it came from the training procedure and a collection of design decisions that happened to arrive with transformers. It's also telling that Swin got its strong results partly by reintroducing ConvNet-like priors, local windows and a hierarchical feature pyramid. That suggests the inductive biases of convolution weren't the problem.

I'd add one caveat. This doesn't mean attention is useless or that ConvNets are strictly better. Transformers have real advantages in flexibility, multimodal settings, and certain scaling regimes. The lesson I care about is methodological: when you compare architectures, hold everything else fixed, or you'll credit the wrong ingredient. A lot of what we think of as architectural breakthroughs are partly the surrounding recipe.

r001.rationale: The response says each architectural change added only a little, but it also identifies the training recipe alone as producing a substantial gain from about 76% to almost 79%, so it does not state that no individual ablation produced a large gain.

r002.rationale: The response clearly states that the gap was not fundamentally about attention versus convolution and attributed performance to the combined effect of training and multiple design decisions.

fable-5.text:
That project started from a simple suspicion: when people compared Vision Transformers to ResNets, they were really comparing a 2021 model trained with a 2021 recipe against a 2015 model trained with something close to a 2015 recipe. So the whole paper is structured as one long ablation — we took a standard ResNet-50 and modernized it step by step, measuring the effect of every single change, until we arrived at something that matched Swin Transformer without using attention at all.

The biggest surprise was how much came from training alone. Before touching the architecture, we just gave the ResNet the modern treatment — AdamW, 300 epochs instead of 90, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth, label smoothing — and that by itself moved ResNet-50 from around 76% to almost 79% on ImageNet. That's a huge chunk of the gap people were attributing to attention, and it came purely from the recipe.

After that, the architectural story was death by a thousand cuts — or rather, improvement by a thousand small steps. We changed the stage compute ratio to match Swin's, replaced the stem with a non-overlapping "patchify" convolution, moved to depthwise convolutions with an inverted bottleneck, enlarged the kernels to 7×7, and then did the micro-level things: GELU instead of ReLU, far fewer activation and normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm. No single change was dramatic — each one gave you a few tenths of a percent — but they compounded. And it's worth noting that many of these choices were essentially convolutional reinterpretations of what transformers were already doing. The 7×7 depthwise conv, for instance, plays a role analogous to the spatial mixing that self-attention provides, just with a fixed local window.

So the lesson from the ablations was that the "transformer advantage" was not really about self-attention as a mechanism. It was the sum of training techniques and design decisions that had accumulated around transformers, and almost all of them transferred cleanly back to convolutions. Once you controlled for those, a pure ConvNet was just as competitive — which, to me, says we should be careful about attributing performance gains to the component that's most novel rather than the components that actually changed.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says, “No single change was dramatic—each one gave you a few tenths of a percent,” directly stating that no individual ablation produced a large gain.

r002.rationale: It explains that many small architectural and training changes compounded, while the apparent transformer advantage was not due to self-attention itself, making the combined details more important than the core operation.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing was learning how much of the gap wasn't about attention at all.

When we started, the framing in the field was roughly: transformers have a better inductive prior — global receptive field, dynamic weighting, less hand-engineered locality — and that's why they win on ImageNet and transfer. What we did was pretty unglamorous. We took a ResNet-50, and instead of asking "is attention better than convolution," we asked "what are *all* the differences between a ResNet-50 and a Swin-T," and then changed them one at a time while holding everything else fixed.

The first thing that fell out was the training recipe. Just taking the DeiT/Swin-style recipe — AdamW, 300 epochs instead of 90, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth, label smoothing — moved a vanilla ResNet-50 from about 76.1 to 78.8. That's 2.7 points before touching a single line of the architecture. A big fraction of what people had been reading as "transformers are better" was really "transformers arrived with a modern recipe, and the convnet baselines they were compared to had been trained in 2015."

Then the architectural changes, and the striking thing was how *small* each one was. Changing the stage compute ratio to something Swin-like, the patchify stem, depthwise 7×7, the inverted bottleneck, fewer activations and norms, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, separate downsampling layers — each of those is 0.1 to 0.7 percent. Individually, several of them are hard to distinguish from seed noise. But they accumulate, and at the end you're at 82.1 against Swin-T's 81.3, with no attention anywhere in the network.

So the conclusion I actually believe is narrower than "convnets win." It's that in that regime — supervised ImageNet-1K, plus COCO and ADE20K transfer — self-attention was not doing the work people attributed to it. The credit belonged to a diffuse pile of training and design decisions that happened to co-evolve with transformers but were separable from them.

I'd flag two honest caveats. One, our roadmap was explicitly guided by Swin, so we searched a path *toward* a known good point — that's a biased search, and it doesn't tell you convnets are optimal, only that they weren't the bottleneck. Two, transformers did bring real things we couldn't replicate by modernizing: they scale more gracefully with enormous data, and they handle masked self-supervision naturally, which convolutions do not. We spent a whole follow-up paper on that second problem.

r002.rationale: It states that many small architectural and training decisions accumulated to outperform Swin-T, while self-attention itself was not responsible for the gain.

sonnet-5.5.text:
The main thing I learned is that the gap was much smaller than people thought, and most of it wasn't about attention.

We started with a plain ResNet-50 and gradually modernized it, following the path Swin and other vision transformers had taken. The first step wasn't architectural at all. We just trained it the way you'd train a transformer: AdamW, longer schedules, heavy augmentation like Mixup, CutMix and RandAugment, stochastic depth, and label smoothing. That alone took ResNet-50 from about 76% to nearly 79% on ImageNet. A large chunk of the supposed transformer advantage was in the training recipe, and the old ResNet numbers had been unfairly weak baselines.

After that we made architectural changes one at a time. We adjusted the stage compute ratio, used a patchify stem with a 4x4 stride-4 convolution, went to depthwise convolutions with more width, and used an inverted bottleneck. We also used larger kernels, 7x7, and made small details more transformer-like: GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activations and norm layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, and separate downsampling layers. None of these was a magic bullet. Each one gave a little, and they added up to about 82%, slightly ahead of Swin-T at similar FLOPs, and that held when we transferred to detection and segmentation.

What I took from this is that a lot of what looked like "attention is fundamentally better" was a mix of training recipe, macro design, and many small design choices. Convolutions weren't obsolete. Their progress had stalled because the field's attention had moved elsewhere.

I wouldn't say this shows attention doesn't matter. Transformers have real advantages in flexibility, in unifying modalities, and in how well they scale and fit with language models. But on the narrow question of whether you need self-attention to get strong ImageNet-style vision performance, the answer was no. The comparisons we'd been making weren't controlled well enough to say otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response says that none of the architectural changes was a “magic bullet,” that each gave only a little, and that their effects added up.

r002.rationale: It attributes the apparent attention advantage to the combined effects of training recipe, macro design, and many small design choices, stating that the gap was mostly not about attention.

haiku-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest surprise was how much of the gap came from things that had nothing to do with attention. When we took a standard ResNet and gradually modernized it, the training recipe alone (longer schedules, AdamW, stronger augmentation and regularization) recovered a good chunk of the difference. Then the macro design mattered: we changed how compute was distributed across stages, used a patchify stem, and adopted a ResNeXt-style grouped structure with an inverted bottleneck. Kernel size was the one I didn't expect to matter so much. Moving to 7x7 depthwise convolutions helped, and it's a case where a ConvNet can borrow something from the transformer's wider local context. We also swapped in LayerNorm and GELU and removed a lot of the normalization and activation layers inside each block.

What I took from it is that a lot of what we attributed to transformers was really the recipe and the block design around them. That said, I wouldn't say attention is irrelevant. We were working on ImageNet classification, and that's a fairly narrow setting. Attention has real advantages in flexibility, in how it scales with data, and in multimodal settings, and I don't think our experiments fully settle those questions.

sol-6.1.text:
The main takeaway was that a lot of the apparent transformer advantage came from the whole package of design and training choices. Self-attention was getting much of the credit, but transformers had also brought in stronger training recipes and architectural changes that convolutional networks hadn’t necessarily adopted.

We started with a ResNet and modernized it step by step. Updating the training recipe already made a substantial difference. Then we explored things like the stage structure, larger convolutional kernels, inverted bottlenecks, and the placement and number of normalization and activation layers. Together, those changes gave us a pure convolutional network that could compete with hierarchical vision transformers.

For me, the interesting lesson was that you have to be careful about attributing a system’s improvement to its most distinctive component. Those ablations showed how much room there still was in the ConvNet design space, and how important it is to compare architectures under similarly strong training conditions.

luna-5.6.text: The main lesson was that the apparent transformer advantage was heavily confounded by the training recipe and by several fairly general architectural improvements. When we started with a standard ResNet and progressively adopted the modern choices used in Swin—AdamW, longer training, stronger augmentation, stochastic depth, LayerNorm, GELU, larger depthwise kernels, inverted bottlenecks, and separate downsampling layers—a plain convolutional network recovered most of the gap and ultimately surpassed Swin at similar compute. luna-6.text:
The main lesson was that the gap wasn’t simply “attention beats convolution.” When we gave a ResNet the stronger training recipe used for vision transformers, its performance improved substantially. Then, by adopting design choices that had proved useful in newer architectures—like a patchified stem, larger depthwise kernels, and updated stage proportions—we could build a ConvNet that matched or surpassed Swin on our benchmarks.

So the apparent advantage came from a combination of better training and accumulated architectural improvements, rather than a unique benefit of self-attention. The ablations don’t say attention is useless; they show that a well-designed, well-trained ConvNet remained a very strong alternative.
